In brief

The fourth theme in the Sirens overture, "Horrid! And gold flushed more," refers to an interaction early in the chapter when Miss Kennedy flushes with embarrassment at Miss Douce's declaration that "I feel all wet." Some readers have heard a lewd double entendre in these words, and the context does perhaps encourage such a reading, but for the two characters, and presumably for many female readers, there is a much more innocuous meaning.

At more length

The barmaids work themselves up into gales of laughter at the goggle-eyed, greasy-nosed, scraggly-bearded "old fogey in Boyd's." When the fit is over Miss Douce says, "I wished I hadn't laughed so much. I feel all wet." Her coworker responds, "You horrid thing! / And flushed yet more (you horrid!), more goldenly." Joyce's commentators and critics tend either to pass over the words "all wet" in decorous silence or briefly note a suggestion of female sexual excitement. Sirens is indeed full of sexual undertones, including many suggestive figures of liquidity and flowing, but please: has anyone ever become sexually excited because she laughed too hard?

I cannot answer my own skeptical question, but I can offer a simpler physiological explanation: when they laugh too hard many women (some sources say as many as half) experience some urinary incontinence. Medical science has identified two ways in which this happens. "Stress incontinence" is the simple result of downward pressure on the bladder. Laughter can bring it on just as coughing or sneezing can. (There are worse effects. Sneezes occasionally rupture eardrums and blood vessels.) Weak pelvic floor muscles make this kind of incontinence more likely, so women who have been through childbirth are prime candidates. The other condition is called "giggle incontinence"—fortuitously, since Joyce uses that word repeatedly in describing the barmaids' laughter ("giggling peal," "bronze gigglegold," "gigglegiggled," "Kennygiggles"). This form of incontinence, less common and less well understood, is thought to involve a neurological reflex that makes the bladder muscles suddenly relax. For some unknown reason it seems to target younger women.

Probably many women feel some embarrassment when urinary incontinence happens to them in a public place, but the daring Miss Douce is not one of them. Her matter-of-fact talk shocks her companion, who experiences an involuntary physiological response of her own, flushing red with embarrassment. Miss Kennedy's "Horrid!" is no different from the response that many readers will have to Bloom's defecation in Calypso. But for Joyce, a literary truth-teller and a former medical student, excretion is a fact of life and should be represented like any other. His eagerness to shock readers, though, begs the question of the other possible meaning of "all wet." While this is surely not the sense that Miss Douce intends or Miss Kennedy hears, narrative context encourages readers to entertain the thought. The two women are laughing at the old pharmacist because he is so unattractive—the very antidote to desire, in their eyes. And that means that sexual desire is on readers' minds when they encounter the phrase.

Something similar happens later in Sirens, when Bloom recalls the night he and Molly gave Ben Dollard a much-too-tight pair of trousers to wear in a concert. The spectacle when he tried on the pants was hilarious: "Molly did laugh when he went out. Threw herself back across the bed, screaming, kicking. With all his belongings on show. O saints above, I'm drenched! O, the women in the front row! O, I never laughed so many!" Here too laughter causes peeing (does "so many" perhaps refer to the number of Molly's convulsive guffaws?), and again the laughter is caused by the sight of a man's body. There is no plausible reason to think that Molly is experiencing desire for Dollard, but the text insinuates such thoughts by describing her laughter as if it were an energetic act of copulation.

The associative linkage seems strange, but perhaps it will appear less puzzling if one considers that the author wrote about undinism and evidently was an undinist himself.

John Hunt 2026
